blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 2 (Bacteria and Viruses), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, compare, label and describe a structure, give examples), as one 4-mark part or in 1+3 / 2+2 sub-parts. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Explain the position of bacteria in the five-kingdom and the three-domain systems of classification, and write the general features of their cellular organization. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Five-kingdom system: proposed by Robert H. Whittaker, it classifies organisms comprehensively in a way that reflects their evolutionary history. The five kingdoms are Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. All prokaryotes are placed in a separate kingdom, Monera; the other four kingdoms include eukaryotes.

Three-domain system: in the last decade molecular studies highlighted serious flaws in the five-kingdom system, and most biologists favour replacing it with the three-domain system, which is more aligned with molecular data. In it, bacteria are prokaryotes classified in a domain of their own, the domain Bacteria.

Cellular organization: bacteria are a diverse group, all with unicellular prokaryotic organization. They lack membrane-bounded organelles, including a well-defined nucleus, and have the simplest cellular organization.

book_ref.quote: This system classified the organisms in a comprehensive way that reflects evolutionary history of organisms

blocks.prompt: 2 Describe the cell membrane and the cytoplasm of a bacterial cell, including mesosomes and ribosomes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cell membrane: the plasma membrane lies just beneath the cell wall; in bacteria that lack a cell wall (mycoplasmas and spiroplasmas) it is the outermost layer. It has no sterols such as cholesterol in its chemical makeup. At some points it invaginates to form vesicles, tubules or lamellae in the cytoplasm, the mesosomes, which take part in DNA replication and cell division and serve as respiratory centres.

Cytoplasm: contains dissolved substances and large structures such as the nucleoid, ribosomes and mesosomes. It lacks a cytoskeleton and membrane-bounded organelles.

Ribosomes: many are freely dispersed in the cytoplasmic matrix and some are loosely attached to the plasma membrane. They are smaller than eukaryotic ribosomes; each sediments at 70S, with a larger 50S and a smaller 30S subunit.

book_ref.quote: These are involved in DNA replication and cell division and also serve as respiratory centres

blocks.prompt: 3 Describe the genetic material of a bacterium. (i) What is the nucleoid and its DNA? (ii) What are plasmids and how are they used in genetic engineering? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Nucleoid: an irregular-shaped dense area near the centre of the cytoplasm that contains DNA. A bacterium has a single, circular, double stranded DNA molecule. It has no attached histones and is sometimes called the chromosome of the bacterium.

(ii) Plasmids: some bacteria also have circular, double-stranded extra chromosomal DNA molecules called plasmids. They are self-replicating and can replicate before or after cell division. They carry genes that enable bacteria to resist unfavourable conditions, e.g., antibiotics.
In genetic engineering, plasmids serve as important vectors: they are used to carry selected genes into bacteria for cloning or for the synthesis of specific proteins.

book_ref.quote: Some bacteria have circular, double-stranded extra chromosomal DNA molecules, called plasmids

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe the chemical nature of the bacterial cell wall. Explain the basis of Gram's staining and write a note on the capsule. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cell wall: a rigid wall around the plasma membrane. Its major component is a unique macromolecule, peptidoglycan or murein, made of long glycan (polysaccharide) chains cross-linked with short peptide fragments. Its amount differs in different bacteria. The wall also contains lipids linked to peptidoglycan.

Gram's staining: devised by Sir Hans Christian Gram. Gram-positive bacteria retain the violet dye and stain purple; Gram-negative bacteria do not retain it and appear in their original colour. This reflects their different walls: Gram-positive walls have a thick peptidoglycan layer and less lipid, while Gram-negative walls have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane of lipopolysaccharides and lipoproteins.

Capsule: some bacteria produce a capsule outside their cell walls. It is a gelatinous layer that gives sticky character to bacterial colonies.

book_ref.quote: It is composed of long glycan (polysaccharide) chain, cross-linked with short peptide fragments

blocks.prompt: 5 What are the functions of flagella? Classify bacteria on the basis of the number and position of flagella. Write a note on pili. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Functions: flagella enable many kinds of bacteria to move; their secondary function is to detect and respond to chemical signals.

Arrangement of flagella:
1. Atrichous: bacteria without flagella.
2. Monotrichous: a single polar flagellum.
3. Lophotrichous: a tuft of flagella at one pole.
4. Amphitrichous: flagella at each of the two poles.
5. Peritrichous: flagella surrounding the whole cell.

Pili (singular pilus): present in some bacteria. They are non-helical, filamentous appendages, smaller and thinner than flagella. Pili are used for attachment of bacteria to various surfaces and are involved in the mating process (conjugation) between cells.

book_ref.quote: Many kinds of bacteria have flagella, which enable them to move

blocks.prompt: 6 Describe the characteristics and importance of omnibacteria, mycoplasmas and spiroplasmas, spirochaetes and pseudomonads. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Omnibacteria: rigid, rod-shaped, heterotrophic, Gram-negative bacteria including many important pathogens. Most have flagella, they do not produce spores and are usually aerobic. Example: Escherichia coli; vibrios are also included.

Mycoplasmas and spiroplasmas: differ from all other bacteria in lacking cell walls, so they resist penicillin and other antibiotics that inhibit cell wall growth. Some mycoplasmas cause diseases in mammals, e.g., certain types of pneumonia in humans; spiroplasmas cause plant diseases, e.g., lethal yellowing of coconuts.

Spirochaetes: long spirilla with Gram-negative walls, with 2 to more than 100 flagella. Treponema is an important spirochaete; it causes syphilis.

Pseudomonads: straight or curved Gram-negative rods with one or many flagella at one end, found in soil and water. They easily break down organic compounds; some are autotrophic, many are plant pathogens and some take part in denitrification. Pseudomonas aeruginosa occurs in soil, water and raw vegetables; usually harmless, it can cause serious infections in weak people.

book_ref.quote: Escherichia coli is an example of such bacteria

blocks.prompt: 7 Describe the cyanobacteria and the actinomycetes, giving their characteristics and importance. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Cyanobacteria: photosynthetic bacteria that played the most important role in Earth's history in increasing free oxygen in the atmosphere. They contain chlorophyll-a and accessory pigments such as carotenoids and blue and red phycobilins. Many fix atmospheric nitrogen in special cells called heterocysts. They are common in soil as mats, occur in lichens on rock surfaces and dominate the mats on sea sediments. Their rampant growth in polluted water forms colourful blooms, coloured by their pigments. The bulk of modern petroleum deposits were formed by masses of decayed cyanobacteria.

Actinomycetes: bacteria with filamentous growth forms that produce spores resistant to unfavourable conditions. Some are nitrogen fixers found in the root nodules of many flowering plants. Some cause dental plaque, in which tooth enamel is destroyed. Mycobacterium leprae causes leprosy and Mycobacterium tuberculosis causes tuberculosis. Many antibiotics, e.g., tetracycline, chloramphenicol, erythromycin and neomycin, were derived originally from actinomycetes, and about 150 new antibiotics from them are discovered each year.

blocks.prompt: 8 Describe the nitrogen-fixing aerobic bacteria and the chemosynthetic bacteria, and explain their role in the nitrogen cycle. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Nitrogen-fixing aerobic bacteria: an economically important group; they are Gram-negative and most are flagellated. Azotobacter is a member; it is found in soil and water and fixes atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia (NH₃). The table lists this group as free-living and mutualistic nitrogen fixers.

Chemosynthetic bacteria: they derive energy from the oxidation of inorganic compounds of nitrogen, sulphur and iron and use it to synthesize their food. Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter belong here. They oxidize nitrogen compounds (NH₃) to gain energy, and the NH₃ is in turn converted to nitrite and nitrate.

Role in the nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixers turn atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia; nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter) turn ammonia into nitrite and nitrate; denitrifying bacteria (Pseudomonas) complete the cycle. Thus bacteria play a vital role in the nitrogen cycle.

book_ref.quote: They oxidize nitrogen compounds (NH₃) to gain energy

blocks.prompt: 9 Explain the role of bacteria (i) as recyclers of nature and (ii) as environmental cleaners. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
(i) Recyclers of nature: bacteria are involved in almost all biogeochemical cycles, in which essential elements move to and fro between organisms and environment.
- Nitrogen cycle: nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) and denitrifying bacteria (Pseudomonas) play a significant role in completing it; nitrogen-fixing Azotobacter supplies ammonia.
- Carbon-hydrogen-oxygen cycle: decomposer bacteria decompose dead organic matter and play a key role.
- Oxygen: photosynthetic bacteria such as cyanobacteria increase free oxygen in the atmosphere.

(ii) Environmental cleaners: many bacteria degrade organic compounds very easily and are used to remove or degrade pollutants from the environment (bioremediation).
- They decompose city sewage into harmless products.
- Bacteria that digest the hydrocarbons in petroleum are used to clean up oil spills.
- They are also used for bioremediation of industrial toxic wastes.

book_ref.quote: The activities of photosynthetic bacteria e.g., cyanobacteria play role in the increase of free oxygen

blocks.prompt: 10 Describe the use of bacteria as makers of useful products and as biopesticides. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Makers of useful products:
- Fermented foods: bacteria such as Lactobacillus, together with yeasts and molds, have been used for thousands of years to prepare cheese, pickles, soy sauce, vinegar, wine and yogurt.
- Chemicals: in the pharmaceutical and agrochemical industry, bacteria are most important in producing important chemicals.
- Antibiotics: some bacteria are used for the production of antibiotics.
- Leather: commercial preparation of animal skins for leather goods involves bacteria.

Biopesticides: bacteria are used in place of pesticides in biological pest control. This commonly involves Bacillus thuringiensis, a Gram-positive, soil dwelling bacterium. These biopesticides are environmentally friendly and have little or no effect on humans, wildlife, pollinators and most other beneficial insects.

book_ref.quote: In pharmaceutical and agrochemical industry, bacteria are most important in the production of important chemicals

blocks.prompt: 11 Where is normal flora found in a healthy animal and what does it consist of? Explain why the association of humans with their normal flora is called mutualistic. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Location: in a healthy animal the internal tissues such as blood, brain and muscle are normally free of microorganisms. Surface tissues such as skin and mucous membranes are constantly in contact with the environment and are colonized by certain microbial species. The mixture of organisms regularly found at any anatomical site is the normal flora.

Composition: bacteria, a few fungi and protists, and some methanogenic archaea; bacteria are the most numerous and obvious.

Mutualism: both partners benefit.
- The flora gets nutrients, a stable environment and constant temperature, protection and transport in the human body.
- The body gets vitamins (e.g., vitamin K and B₁₂ from enteric bacteria), protection because the flora competes with pathogens for attachment sites and nutrients and makes substances that inhibit or kill them, and cross-reactive antibodies that help prevent infection.

book_ref.quote: are constantly in contact with environment and are colonized by certain microbial species

blocks.prompt: 12 Describe the general structure of a virus: its size, core, capsid, envelope and shapes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Size: viruses are extremely small infectious agents, seen only under an electron microscope. They range from 20 nm (parvovirus) to 250 nm (pox viruses) and are 10 to 1000 times smaller than most bacteria.

Core: the central core is the genome, made of nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA.

Capsid: a protein coat around the core that gives definite shape to the virus. It is made of protein subunits called capsomeres; their number and kind are characteristic of a virus (herpes virus 162, adenovirus 252). Core and capsid together form the nucleocapsid.

Envelope: in some animal viruses only, the nucleocapsid is covered by a lipid-rich membrane derived from the host cell. Non-enveloped viruses are naked viruses.

Shapes: animal and plant viruses may be polyhedron (many sides) or helical; bacteriophages may be cubical, icosahedral (20 faces), helical, or complex (polyhedral head and rod-shaped tail).

book_ref.quote: The central core of a virus is its genome

blocks.prompt: 13 What are bacteriophages? Explain how bacteriophages are used as carriers in genetic engineering to make transgenic bacteria. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Bacteriophages are a diverse group of viruses that attack bacteria; they are among the most complex viruses. The best known phages of Escherichia coli are the T-phages. A T4 phage has a head, whose protein capsid encloses a long double stranded DNA, and a tail whose six tail fibres help it attach to the bacterial wall.

Use as carriers:
1. The gene of interest is inserted into the DNA of the bacteriophage.
2. The phage carries this DNA to the target bacterial cell.
3. When the virus incorporates its DNA into the bacterial chromosome, the gene of interest also becomes a part of the bacterial DNA.
4. Such bacteria are transgenic, i.e., their genome has DNA of some other organism. They can be grown to get copies of the gene of interest and to obtain the required protein.

book_ref.quote: Bacteriophages are used as carriers in genetic engineering

blocks.prompt: 14 What are retroviruses? Explain reverse transcription. Write the history of the discovery of AIDS and why the disease is fatal. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Retroviruses: a special group of animal viruses to which HIV belongs. They contain RNA and capsids surrounded by lipid-rich envelopes bearing glycoprotein spikes that help the virus identify and bind to its target. They are spherical and about 100 nm in diameter.

Reverse transcription: the most distinguishing character of retroviruses is the enzyme reverse transcriptase. It catalyses reverse transcription, in which single stranded RNA is reversely transcribed into a strand of DNA; the enzyme then uses this DNA strand to complete a double helix of DNA.

History of AIDS: AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) was first reported in 1981; later it was found in patients who had received blood or blood products from AIDS patients. In 1984 its agent was found to be a virus, and in 1986 the virus was named Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). HIV is host specific: it multiplies in monkeys but does not cause AIDS in them.

Why fatal: AIDS weakens the immune system, and no one can survive without an immune system to defend against other viral and bacterial infections.

book_ref.quote: This enzyme catalyses the process of reverse transcription
